raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed distal opacification of one or more epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of flow-limiting stenosis, dissection, thrombus, ectasia, spasm, or severe myocardial/valvular disease. It was first described in patients with angina and angiographically “normal” coronary arteries [1]. Objective diagnosis generally uses the corrected thrombolysis in myocardial infarction frame count (cTFC), a reproducible index of contrast transit; many studies define slow flow as cTFC >27 frames, or >2 standard deviations above normal for a given vessel [2]. CSFP should be distinguished from no-reflow after myocardial infarction or percutaneous coronary intervention, and from secondary slow flow due to diffuse obstructive disease, ectasia, embolization, high filling pressures, or technical angiographic factors.

CSFP is not simply a benign angiographic curiosity. Histopathological studies have shown small-vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, endothelial swelling, and patchy myocardial abnormalities, supporting a microvascular substrate [3,4]. Clinically, patients often present with recurrent rest angina, mixed angina, abnormal stress tests, acute coronary syndrome–like presentations, and repeated hospital visits despite the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease [5]. Observational series suggest a prevalence of approximately 1–7% among patients undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography, with associations including male sex, smoking, obesity, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [6]. Because definitions vary, Beltrame emphasized the need for standardized angiographic criteria and exclusion of confounders before labeling primary CSFP [7]. Contemporary reviews frame CSFP within ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries, while retaining its distinctive angiographic phenotype [8-11].

Pathophysiology is multifactorial. Invasive hemodynamic studies by Beltrame and colleagues demonstrated increased resting microvascular tone, abnormal endothelial responses, and evidence of inducible ischemia, supporting a coronary microvascular disorder [12]. Fineschi and colleagues reported preserved coronary flow reserve despite increased resting microvascular resistance, implying that slow resting contrast passage does not necessarily equate to impaired hyperemic reserve [13]. This distinction was reinforced in a large contemporary INOCA cohort in which angiographic slow flow correlated only weakly with invasively measured coronary flow reserve and index of microcirculatory resistance, cautioning against using cTFC alone as a surrogate for coronary microvascular dysfunction [14].

Endothelial dysfunction is a central mechanism. Peripheral flow-mediated dilation is impaired in CSFP, suggesting systemic endothelial involvement rather than an isolated coronary abnormality [15]. Intravascular ultrasound and fractional flow reserve studies have also identified diffuse intimal thickening, calcification, and increased epicardial resistance in some patients, raising the possibility that CSFP may represent early or diffuse atherosclerosis not appreciated by luminography [16]. Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, neurohumoral imbalance, and abnormal vasoactive peptides have been reported; low plasma nitric oxide relates inversely to TIMI frame count [17], and altered endothelial markers such as ghrelin have also been examined [18]. Hemorheologic and platelet abnormalities may contribute, with increased platelet volume indices supporting a prothrombotic or platelet-activation component [19]. Electrical consequences are clinically relevant: heterogeneity in slow flow among vessels correlates with P-wave dispersion [20], and increased QT dispersion has been reported, providing a mechanistic link to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias [21].

Treatment remains empirical because randomized trials are few and outcomes data are limited. Therapy begins with confirmation of the diagnosis, exclusion of secondary causes, and aggressive management of cardiovascular risk factors—smoking cessation, weight reduction, blood pressure control, lipid lowering, exercise, and treatment of diabetes or sleep apnea. Nitrates may help some patients but are often inconsistent, presumably because the dominant abnormality resides in resistance vessels rather than epicardial tone. Case observations implicate contrast-induced microvascular spasm in some patients [22]. Oral dipyridamole has been reported to improve angiographic flow [23], and the T-type calcium-channel blocker mibefradil improved angiographic and clinical parameters before market withdrawal [24]. Nicorandil improves acute frame counts more than nitrates in small studies [25] and may improve myocardial function while favorably modulating nitric oxide and endothelin-1 [26]. Among more practical options, diltiazem improved coronary flow, exercise tolerance, and angina in a randomized double-blind trial [27], and intracoronary diltiazem acutely reduced frame counts more than nitroglycerin in selected patients [28]. Intracoronary nicardipine has also been used to reverse spontaneous CSFP [29]. Statins may be useful beyond lipid lowering, with atorvastatin improving coronary flow and endothelial markers in a small study [30].

In summary, CSFP is a reproducible angiographic syndrome with important symptomatic, ischemic, and arrhythmic implications. Its substrate is heterogeneous—microvascular constriction, endothelial dysfunction, diffuse atherosclerosis, inflammation, platelet activation, and autonomic or vasospastic mechanisms may predominate in different patients. Future work should standardize diagnostic thresholds, incorporate invasive and non-invasive coronary function testing, and test mechanism-targeted therapies in adequately powered trials.
